newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends mixed, French franc slumps.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends mixed, French franc slumps.

text.p: The dollar rose against the French franc Thursday amid signs of growing displeasure in France with the planned single European currency, but ended little changed against most other major currencies.

A poll showed most French voters believe European Monetary Union will hurt jobs and economic growth and 69 percent want a fresh vote on the single currency project, which France narrowly approved in 1992.

Rejection of the monetary union, which would combine the French franc with the traditionally stronger German mark and other European currencies, could spark heavy selling of francs for marks and dollars, traders said.

"I still think there's some pretty good risk in France. To me, the uncertainty hasn't yet been priced in in this market," said Mark Gargano, managing director of currency derivatives at First Union National Bank.

French President Jacques Chirac on Monday called parliamentary elections on May 25 and June 1, nine months ahead of schedule. Analysts said that was an effort to head off rising opposition to the planned single currency.

The mark also gained on the opposition registered in the French poll since many investors believe the planned single currency, to be called the euro, would weaken the German economy and hurt the mark.
That kept a lid on the dollar, which had risen against the mark early in European trading.

"If France decides EMU is a non-starter, we're going to throw the whole thing out and that would temper upward dollar momentum," said Diego Giurleo, vice president of treasury at Royal Bank of Canada in New York.
The dollar rose to 5.7855 French francs late in New York, from 5.7785 late on Wednesday. The dollar was little changed at 1.7147 marks, compared to 1.7146, and at 126.10 Japanese yen, from 126.05.
The British pound rose to $1.6260 from $1.6233. The dollar fell to Canadian $1.3928 from C$1.3932.

The dollar rose toward 1.72 marks after Germany reported that inflation fell in April. Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp said he saw no current inflation danger, but noted that any cuts in interest rates would be risky now.
Steady German rates, when rates are generally expected to rise in the United States, would tend to enhance the dollar's value.
Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer later echoed Krupp's comments, adding that he was generally satisfied with current foreign exchange rates.
The dollar got a small boost against the yen in late New York trading on a Japanese news report that Japan's Ministry of Finance was set to order the closure of Nissan Mutual Life Insurance Co.
That would be the first time since World War II that a Japanese life insurer had failed and the report deepened fears about Japan's prolonged economic malaise.
"It's not a really big company, but the dollar was well-bid against the yen after the news," said Masashi Ehara, assistant vice president in foreign exchange at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.

Dealers said trading volume was light. Few investors were willing to make aggressive bets on the dollar ahead of a meeting on Friday between President Clinton and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.

In addition, investors awaited a Sunday meeting of economic officials of the Group of Seven wealthy industrial nations, which some feared might produce a statement calling for the dollar to weaken versus the yen.
"A big fear of intervention remains in the marketplace and that's effectively negative for the dollar," said Giurleo.
